title: Bernstein-Vazirani Networks: Quantum Machine Learning by Interference
authors: Natacha Kuete Meli, Tolga Birdal, Prayag Tiwari, Vladislav Golyanik, Michael Moeller
abstract: We introduce Bernstein-Vazirani Networks (BVNs), a non-variational quantum machine learning framework that leverages quantum interference for supervised learning, demonstrated on vision and representation learning tasks. In their standard form, BVNs follow the principle of quantum Fourier sampling: labelled data are placed in superposition and interfered in the Fourier basis to extract globally informative features. We then define generalised BVNs that enable interference in problem-adapted bases, yielding more expressive models under the same measurement budget as in the standard setting. BVNs achieve universal function approximation through (over)complete interference bases, while training of BVNs is gradient-free. Experiments on synthetic and real-world classification tasks, as well as implicit image representation, show strong generalisation capabilities and competitive performance with classical and quantum baselines.
summary: This paper introduces Bernstein-Vazirani Networks (BVNs), a non-variational quantum machine learning framework that uses quantum interference for supervised learning. By generalizing the standard BV algorithm, the authors create more expressive models capable of handling complex data structures without relying on gradient optimization. This offers a promising, efficient alternative to current PQC methods for quantum data processing.
main_problem: To develop Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models that overcome the architectural and trainability challenges associated with existing approaches, particularly Parametrised Quantum Circuits (PQCs).
main_result: The proposed Bernstein-Vazirani Networks (BVNs) achieve strong generalization capabilities and competitive performance on real-world tasks while remaining gradient-free and more sampling-efficient than PQC models.
method: The framework uses quantum interference, generalizing the standard Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm by introducing task-adaptive basis functions and expressive input representations to encode complex data structures.
model_or_system: The model is a quantum circuit architecture (BVN) that processes labelled data by placing it in superposition and interfering the resulting states in a problem-adapted basis, avoiding the need for classical outer-loop optimization.
key_observables: Accuracy (Acc.) on classification tasks, measurement distribution sparsity, and the ability to reconstruct coefficients in closed form.
important_parameters: The measurement budget, the choice of interference operator (Hadamard, Chebyshev, Fourier), and the regularization factor $\lambda$.
main_assumptions: The authors address the 'leakage' problem and assume that generalizing the interference mechanism allows for universal function approximation without relying on gradient descent.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison between standard and generalized BVNs for 2D point classification, showing improved decision boundaries and better fitting of target functions compared to standard models.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from introducing the limitations of PQCs, detailing the standard BVN mechanism, generalizing it with task-adaptive bases, and finally testing the enhanced model on synthetic and real-world datasets (Iris, Penguins).
why_interesting: The work provides a quantum algorithm paradigm for ML that bypasses the gradient-based optimization issues (like barren plateaus) plaguing many current quantum simulation and computation approaches.

figures.caption: Figure 1. The proposed standard (1a) and generalised (1b) Bernstein–Vazirani Networks (BVNs). In the standard setting, binary inputs xi are linearly combined in a hidden layer with optimised binary weights yj, passed through a parity activation χ, and linearly combined at the output layer using Fourier coefficients bf(yj). In the generalised setting, inputs pass through expressive optimised sub-models χ (cartooned in the red box) before the output combination, enabling richer representations. Figure 2. The Bernstein–Vazirani algorithm (Bernstein & Vazirani, 1993). The algorithm mainly consists of three steps: (i) initialise the system in a perfect superposition; (ii) call the function oracle; (iii) apply the Hadamard operator for interference. If ˜f satisfies the promise ˜f(x) = s ⊙x, measuring reveals s with certainty.

Figure 3. Our generalised Bernstein–Vazirani algorithm. We use three quantum registers: An input register, a register that computes a weighted representation of the inputs, and a weight register controlling this representation. The algorithm has three stages: (i) Prepare a uniform superposition of all inputs (Prep.) and weight configurations, and compute the representations; (ii) Query the oracle encoding the ground-truth labels across all samples in the superposition; (iii) Apply an interference operator so the labels interfere with the basis functions generated by the representation.

Figure 5. Real-world classification results on Iris and Penguins datasets, with filled vs. unfilled (original) comparison for BVNs. Filled data substantially improves the generalised BVN, allowing >90% accuracy with only 25% data, comparable to the baselines.

Figure 6. Implicit image representation. The top row shows results on the coarse (64×64) training image, while the bottom row shows evaluations on a finer (128×128) test image. The generalised BVN outperforms the standard BVN and is competitive with the benchmarks.
